title: Swift Is Working Again, and Falling
hook: NASA has revived two of Swift's telescopes after a failed commercial reboost attempt. The problem now is not electronics but air: atmospheric drag is pulling the observatory down faster than expected.
key_points: Two of the ageing Swift observatory's telescopes are back online after technical problems.
A commercial mission meant to raise its orbit and extend its life was derailed.
Even in low Earth orbit there is enough residual air to sap orbital energy — drag.
Swift is descending faster than predicted, so it may have only a month or two of useful altitude left.
Below a critical altitude the spacecraft can no longer point and operate reliably.
content_html: Swift has been NASA's fast-reflex eye on the violent sky for two decades, swinging onto gamma-ray bursts within a minute of detecting them. After technical trouble, NASA has now brought two of its telescopes back online — but the reprieve may be brief.
extra_html: A commercial mission intended to rescue the ageing spacecraft by raising its orbit was derailed, and Swift is still subject to the slow grind that limits every low-Earth-orbit satellite: the atmosphere does not simply stop, it thins out. The residual air at orbital altitude drags on the spacecraft, converting orbital energy into heat and lowering the orbit. According to ScienceDaily, that descent is running faster than expected, leaving perhaps another month or two before Swift drops below the altitude at which it can operate. Without a successful reboost, one of the most productive transient-hunting observatories in astronomy runs out of sky.

related.title: Fast Radio Bursts Follow Star Formation Almost Instantly
related.hook: Mysterious millisecond flashes from across the universe closely track where new stars are being born — with almost no time lag, ruling out one of the leading theories of what causes them.

related.title: Astronomers Caught a Magnetar Being Born
related.hook: A supernova's light curve started 'chirping' — bumps in brightness arriving closer and closer together — the birth cry of one of the universe's most extreme objects: a magnetar.

flashcards.prompt: Why does a satellite in low Earth orbit lose altitude over time?

choices.text: Residual atmosphere at orbital altitude produces drag, bleeding off orbital energy
Earth's gravity strengthens the longer a satellite orbits
Solar radiation pressure always pushes satellites downward

flashcards.explanation_html: Low Earth orbit is not a vacuum. The thin remaining air exerts drag, so without periodic reboosts the orbit decays — which is exactly what is now threatening Swift.

flashcards.prompt: What was the commercial mission to Swift meant to accomplish?
flashcards.back_html: Raise the ageing observatory's orbit to counter atmospheric drag and extend its operating life. It ran into technical problems and did not succeed.
